Subject: Quick clarifying examples on billing for short bursts / merged contexts

Thanks again for the demo earlier. Procurement wants concrete examples we can reconcile against an invoice: when multiple very short calls from our app occur within a short window, how will those be billed? Specific asks below:

1) If three separate API calls each generate a ~25-token completion (and each uses the same cached 200-token system prompt), do we pay the minimum per-call or is there aggregation?
2) For streaming responses where the client opens a stream and receives 1–2 tokens at a time, is each flush considered a billable call?
3) If we do a merge on our side (client concatenates history before calling), is that charged differently than individual calls that the platform merges via prefix/KV cache?

Can you send a sample invoice line (or two) showing the math? Procurement would like enough detail to reconcile next week's billing.

Samir —

Thanks for the clear asks. Below are our operational billing rules and three concise invoice-style examples so your procurement/finance team can reconcile quickly. I attached a one‑page "sample_invoice_lines.pdf" and a small workbook with the math.

Key rules (short):
- Unit: billable tokens (input + output) counted at model tokenization.
- Rounding granularity: 10-token units (bill up to the next 10 tokens).
- Per-request minimum: 30 billable tokens if the request originates as a distinct API call (this protects against very short chat pings).
- Session/window aggregation: calls from the same API key + conversation id are aggregated into a single billing session when they occur within a 10-minute sliding window; aggregated billable tokens are summed before applying rounding and minimums.
- KV / prefix caching: when the runtime detects a cached prefix reused across calls during the window, we exclude the cached prefix tokens from billable input for repeated identical prefixes (i.e., you are not charged repeatedly for the same system prompt across aggregated calls).
- Streaming: tokenization happens at server-side emission; multiple flushes within a single logical request are treated as part of the same request and do not trigger multiple minima. However, separate HTTP requests/streams are separate calls.

Example 1 — three separate short calls (no aggregation):
- Each call: prompt 200-token cached prefix (reused), variable input 10 tokens, completion 25 tokens.
- Billable per call: input (10) + output (25) = 35 -> rounded up to 40 (10-token granularity), meets per-request minimum 30 so 40 tokens billed per call.
- Total invoice line: 3 calls * 40 tokens = 120 tokens billed.

Example 2 — three calls inside 10-minute window, session aggregation applies, prefix cached:
- Same token counts as above, but calls share conversation id and occur within 10 minutes. We sum billable tokens across calls: (10+25) * 3 = 105 raw tokens -> rounding to nearest 10 -> 110 tokens billed (aggregation bypasses per-call minimums; the per-request minimum is only enforced for isolated calls outside a session).

Example 3 — mix of streaming and direct calls:
- Call A: streaming response, single connection, total emitted tokens 18 (output) + 12 input = 30 raw -> rounding -> 30 (already at minimum). Single request minimum satisfied.
- Call B: separate HTTP request 2 minutes later, small 8-token output + 12 input = 20 raw -> rounded to 20 but per-request minimum 30 applies (if not aggregated) -> 30 billed.
- If A and B are same conversation id within 10 minutes, we aggregate: A(30) + B(20) = 50 -> rounded -> 50 billed (no per-request minimum reapplication).

Notes on invoice presentation:
- We will show an invoice line per billing session id when aggregation occurs, with a brief note: "Aggregated session (10-min window) — calls: N, raw_tokens: X, rounded_tokens: Y".
- Isolated calls appear as their own lines and show the applied per-request minimum when it triggers.

Next steps / proposal:
- I included a sample invoice (sample_invoice_lines.pdf). If procurement prefers a different window (e.g., 5 or 15 minutes) for the pilot, we can negotiate it into the pilot terms — it affects the degree of aggregation and therefore billed tokens.
- We can also offer a pilot credit: first-month aggregation audit with a 20% credit on billed tokens for customers migrating from another provider, so you can reconcile technical vs. expected numbers.

If you want, Ben (cc'd) can provide a quick breakdown of how rounding interacts with seat/commit tiers for your quoted plan; Rafael can follow up on updating the SOW language for the pilot if you accept the credit.

Adding two quick clarifications from pricing ops so procurement has predictable language:

- Rounding is always upwards (ceiling) to the next 10-token bucket. So 101 tokens -> 110 billed.
- For metered commit customers we apply rounding and aggregation before we compare against committed units; e.g., commits are decremented by billed (rounded) tokens.

Small table (inline):
- Scenario A (isolated tiny call): raw 22 -> ceil-> 30 -> billed 30.
- Scenario B (aggregate 3 calls, raw 105) -> ceil -> 110 billed.

These points will appear on the detailed invoice/supplemental CSV export so finance teams can reconcile line-by-line.
